messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Miguel Rivas, a 67-year-old single Latino physician, came to treatment after years of carrying the aftermath of the night his young son nearly died from a sudden, terrifying illness. Miguel had been at home when the boy became violently unwell, first looking pale and weak, then deteriorating so quickly that the evening became a blur of urgent calls, hospital corridors, and moments when Miguel felt he was watching his child slip away in front of him. What stayed with him most was not a complete sequence but fragments: the sound of a monitor, a doctor’s voice, his son’s small body, his own hands shaking while trying to stay useful. He said he knew what had happened, but when he tried to tell it, the story came out broken and incomplete, as if the rest of it had vanished. Even now, he felt unable to find the words for it; he could describe pieces, but not make them into a clear account, not even to himself.

In the months that followed, Miguel began trying hard not to think about the trauma at all. He threw himself into work, kept his schedule full, and filled every quiet moment with charts, calls, and paperwork so his mind would not have room to drift back to that night. When the memory did intrude, he would push it away, telling himself that thinking about it served no purpose. The more he avoided it, the more the memory seemed to fray. He noticed that the details became even less organized, as if each deliberate push away left him with only another shard and made the whole event harder to hold together. He could still sense that something terrible had happened, but the harder he tried not to remember, the more the memory seemed to lose its shape, until it felt less like a story than a cluster of disconnected moments.

What made avoidance feel necessary was the sense of threat that had never fully left him. Miguel remained superalert, scanning hospital waiting rooms, news reports, and even ordinary conversations for signs that something similar might be happening again. If a child coughed in a clinic, or a family member sounded tired on the phone, he would feel his body tense and his attention sharpen at once. At times, a flash of the old fear would come over him so vividly that he felt as if he were back in that emergency room again, hearing the same urgency in the air and reliving the helplessness of not knowing whether his son would survive. The feelings that came with those moments were intense and painful—fear, horror, guilt, and shame all mixed together—and they kept him on guard.

That constant watchfulness, in turn, fed his efforts to keep his mind occupied all the time. Miguel noticed that whenever he allowed himself even a little stillness, the images and sensations came back more easily, along with the abrupt rush of dread. So he kept moving, kept working, and kept his attention fixed outward, as though vigilance could protect him and distraction could keep the past from taking over. But this way of living also made the memory feel more fragmented and harder to narrate, because he never stayed with it long enough to organize it. In that sense, his effort to escape the experience of the event seemed to keep the event alive in pieces: the more he suppressed it and avoided thinking about it, the less coherent it became, and the less coherent it became, the more frightening it felt to approach.

As a physician, Miguel found this especially painful in his daily environment. He would stand in exam rooms with families and children, outwardly composed, while privately bracing himself whenever he heard a worried parent mention fever, weakness, or a sudden change in a child’s condition. He began avoiding any unnecessary exposure to pediatric cases and cutting short conversations that might open the door to what happened with his son. The consequences reached beyond work; he became more withdrawn and less available to the few people who tried to ask how he was doing. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the effort of staying busy, frightened by how quickly the old scene could return, and ashamed that he still could not tell the story clearly. What finally brought him in was the fear that he would remain trapped between fragments of memory and constant watchfulness, and his hope was that he might finally understand what happened well enough to stop living as if it were about to happen again.
